analysis.one_liner: Taxes the net wealth of America's richest households at up to 8% a year.
analysis.headline: The wealth tax bill, introduced with 22 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support, was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would put a new annual tax on wealth itself, not just income. Households and trusts with net worth above a high threshold — 1,000 times the greater of $50,000 or the median American household's wealth, which puts it in the neighborhood of the richest few thousand households — would pay 2% to 8% of their net value each year, with the rate rising as wealth rises. Ordinary households' assets are largely excluded, and the IRS would have to audit at least 30% of wealth-tax payers annually with steeper penalties for undervaluing assets.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, the general public would benefit from revenue raised exclusively from households and trusts at the very top of the wealth distribution — a pool of wealth that currently escapes income tax year after year because gains on assets that are never sold are not taxed. Most other taxpayers would owe nothing under the new tax, since property worth $50,000 or less and most tangible personal property is excluded.

how_it_helps.text: The bill imposes an annual tax of 2% to 8% on the net value of a taxpayer's assets above a threshold set at 1,000 times the greater of $50,000 or the median household wealth of the United States, with rates stepping up as wealth increases.
Ordinary property is largely carved out: assets worth $50,000 or less and most tangible personal property are excluded from the tax base.
The IRS must audit at least 30% of wealth-tax payers every year and the bill adds enhanced penalties for understating the value of property, aiming at assets that are hard to value or easy to hide.
Taxpayers with severe liquidity constraints — for example, someone whose wealth is tied up in a private business — may defer payment for up to five years.

analysis.who_pays: Individuals and trusts whose net wealth exceeds roughly $200 million (1,000 times the median household's wealth). A household right at the threshold would pay 2% of its value above it each year, and the marginal rate rises to 4%, 6%, and 8% at higher levels of wealth; trusts pay 8% above the threshold. Family wealth held in trusts is attributed back to grantors and beneficiaries and taxed.
analysis.who_pays_short: Households worth roughly $200 million or more

drawbacks.text: Valuing assets that are not publicly traded — private companies, real estate, art — every year is genuinely hard; the bill directs the Treasury to write new formulaic valuation methods, which would be contentious and could produce disputed bills.
The bill does not direct the new revenue to any specific use, so any benefit to ordinary people depends entirely on future congressional decisions about how the money is spent.

Rates of up to 8% of net wealth per year are far steeper than any existing U.S. tax on wealth, and the bill's own structure anticipates pushback: it adds an exit-style tax for covered expatriates as if their tax year ended the day before they renounce citizenship.

The tax would face serious constitutional questions, since the Constitution has historically been read to require that direct taxes be apportioned among the states; an annual tax on unrealized asset value is the kind of tax those questions center on.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea is straightforward: tax wealth at the very top that currently goes largely untaxed because unsold assets never trigger income tax. The design is aggressive — rates far above any existing wealth tax, and an annual valuation regime for private assets that would be expensive and litigious. Supporters would say steep rates and strict valuation rules are what make the tax collectible at all; skeptics would say the valuation machinery and constitutional risk mean the bill, if enacted, would raise less and fight more than its sponsors project. The bill's biggest practical weakness is that it does not say what the money would fund.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up; it sat there until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Barbara Lee introduced the Oligarch Act of 2023 on July 26, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
Twenty-two House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote — the bill's last action was its referral to committee.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill expired in committee without any vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households with fortunes at or above the tax's threshold are better off: they continue to pay no annual tax on their wealth, and gains on assets they never sell remain untaxed. The committee that declined to act avoided the fight over a steep new tax.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ultrawealthy households and the committee that never acted

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors were House Democrats and the sponsor is a Democrat; no Republican signed on, and with Republicans controlling the House and its tax committee, the bill never advanced.

industries.note: The bill would impose an annual tax of up to 8% of net wealth on fortunes above roughly $200 million, a pool of wealth that currently pays no tax on gains until assets are sold. Households at this level had a direct financial stake in the bill never moving.
The bill taxes trusts at 8% and attributes trust assets back to grantors and beneficiaries, targeting vehicles commonly used to shelter family wealth across generations.

The bill authorizes the Treasury to impose reporting duties on financial institutions and business entities, including estimates of a business's own value, to enforce the tax — a compliance burden, not a business threat.
